name: dialogue_mechanics
description: The mechanical layer of dialogue on the page: attribution tags and action beats, speech typography and punctuation, exchange shapes, subtext technique, and the rendering of silence.

tags_and_beats.name: said as the invisible tag
tags_and_beats.definition: Using 'said' as the default attribution verb, on the principle that readers process it as punctuation rather than as a word.
tags_and_beats.example: "The March file is gone," she said. "I looked twice."
tags_and_beats.effect: Attributes without adding a second performance on top of the line; the dialogue keeps the reader's whole attention.
tags_and_beats.caution: Invisible is not free — three 'saids' in four consecutive short lines start to be heard. Alternate with beats and untagged lines.

tags_and_beats.name: asked as the second invisible tag
tags_and_beats.definition: The small closed set of tag verbs that stay transparent alongside 'said' — asked, told, replied in moderation, and volume verbs like whispered and shouted when the volume is genuine information.
tags_and_beats.example:
"Who signed for it?" she asked.
"Nobody," he whispered. "That's the point."
tags_and_beats.effect: Carries a grammatical or acoustic fact the line cannot carry itself, without editorializing.
tags_and_beats.caution: 'Replied', 'answered', and 'responded' are already at the edge; past three in a chapter they read as a thesaurus at work.

tags_and_beats.name: said-bookism
tags_and_beats.definition: Replacing 'said' with an ostentatious substitute — expostulated, opined, ejaculated, riposted — in flight from repetition.
tags_and_beats.example: Weak: "You cannot be serious," he expostulated. Fixed: "You cannot be serious." He put down the fork.
tags_and_beats.effect: Drags the reader's eye off the line and onto the narrator's vocabulary.
tags_and_beats.caution: The instinct behind it is right — the repetition was real; the fix is a beat or no tag at all, not a longer verb.

tags_and_beats.name: adverb-loaded tag
tags_and_beats.definition: A tag that supplies with an adverb the emotion the quoted line should have earned on its own.
tags_and_beats.example: Weak: "I don't care what it costs," she said angrily. Fixed: "I don't care what it costs." She said it twice, the second time to the window.
tags_and_beats.effect: Tells the reader the reading rather than letting the line produce it; the adverb usually marks a line that is not yet doing its job.
tags_and_beats.caution: The rare keeper is the adverb that contradicts the line ('"Fine," she said pleasantly') — there the adverb is information, not commentary.

tags_and_beats.name: non-speech verb as tag
tags_and_beats.definition: Attaching the quotation to a verb that cannot produce articulated speech — laughed, smiled, grinned, shrugged, sighed — as though it were a speech verb.
tags_and_beats.example: Weak: "Forget it," he laughed. Fixed: "Forget it." He laughed, and did not look at her.
tags_and_beats.effect: Reads as a mechanical impossibility to attentive readers; the fix is one period, which also gives the beat its own weight.
tags_and_beats.caution: 'Sighed' and 'breathed' pass in some commercial registers; check the house style before hunting them all.

tags_and_beats.name: beat-for-tag substitution
tags_and_beats.definition: Attributing a line by placing the speaker's physical action in the same paragraph instead of a reporting clause, so paragraph adjacency does the work the tag would have done.
tags_and_beats.example: "That is not my signature." She turned the page face down and left it there.
tags_and_beats.effect: Attributes, paces, and characterizes in one stroke, and puts a body in a scene that was becoming voices only.
tags_and_beats.caution: The beat must belong to the speaker — an action by the other party in the same paragraph reassigns the line without meaning to.

tags_and_beats.name: gesture beat
tags_and_beats.definition: A beat built from the speaker's body — hands, gaze, posture — chosen because it is legible from outside and specific to that character.
tags_and_beats.example: "We can revisit it in the spring." He squared the papers against the desk, edge by edge, until they were a block.
tags_and_beats.effect: Gives the line a physical tempo and lets the body dissent from the words.
tags_and_beats.caution: Nodding, shrugging, and smiling are the three gestures every draft overuses; if the beat could belong to anyone, it belongs to no one.

tags_and_beats.name: prop beat
tags_and_beats.definition: A beat routed through an object the scene has already established — a cup, a phone, a folder — so the action carries the scene's own furniture.
tags_and_beats.example: "I never saw the second invoice." She set the cup down on the ring it had already made.
tags_and_beats.effect: Attributes while advancing the scene's physical situation; props accumulate meaning across a chapter in a way gestures do not.
tags_and_beats.caution: Props must have been placed before they are used, or the beat reads as a set dressed mid-take.

tags_and_beats.name: interior-thought beat
tags_and_beats.definition: A line of the viewpoint character's interiority placed between two spoken lines, doing the attributing and supplying the gap between what is thought and what is said.
tags_and_beats.example:
"Of course. Whatever's easiest."
It was not what was easiest. It was what would take longest to undo.
"Then we'll leave it as it is," he said.
tags_and_beats.effect: Opens the distance between the said and the meant — the cheapest subtext available in close third or first person.
tags_and_beats.register: close third and first person only
tags_and_beats.caution: Available to one character only; a thought beat for the non-viewpoint speaker is a point-of-view break.

tags_and_beats.name: contradicting beat
tags_and_beats.definition: A beat whose physical content argues against the line it accompanies, so the reader believes the body over the words.
tags_and_beats.example: "I'm not upset." She was still holding the phone she had put down twice.
tags_and_beats.effect: Manufactures subtext out of two neutral elements; neither line nor beat has to be clever.
tags_and_beats.caution: Once per exchange. A scene in which every beat contradicts every line becomes a wink at the reader.

tags_and_beats.name: inert beat
tags_and_beats.definition: A beat that occupies a line without characterizing, pacing, or contradicting — sipping, nodding, looking up, crossing the room for no reason.
tags_and_beats.example: Weak: "I'll think about it." He nodded. "Good," she said, nodding. Fixed: "I'll think about it." "That's not a yes."
tags_and_beats.effect: Costs a line and returns nothing; a page of inert beats reads as choreography notes.
tags_and_beats.caution: Test: delete the beat. If nothing is lost but the attribution, use 'said' instead.

tags_and_beats.name: rhythm-reset beat
tags_and_beats.definition: A deliberately longer beat dropped into a fast exchange to reset the tempo before the next volley.
tags_and_beats.example:
"You knew."
"I knew what was in the file."
"You knew."
Outside, a truck backed up somewhere behind the building, beeping, for a long time.
"I knew," he said.
tags_and_beats.effect: Buys silence without a paragraph break and makes the line after it land harder for having been waited for.
tags_and_beats.caution: Use the room, not the character — a beat about the speaker's feelings at this point deflates the pressure the exchange built.

tags_and_beats.name: beat splitting the line
tags_and_beats.definition: An action beat inserted inside a single character's utterance, breaking the quotation into two sentences rather than interrupting a clause.
tags_and_beats.example: "I read the whole thing." She turned the folder around so it faced him. "Twice."
tags_and_beats.effect: Places a pause exactly where the speaker's attention moves, and gives the second half the weight of an afterthought.
tags_and_beats.caution: Distinct from the medial tag: the beat needs its own full stop, because an action is not a reporting clause.

tags_and_beats.name: front-loaded tag
tags_and_beats.definition: Attribution placed before the quoted line, so the reader knows the speaker going in.
tags_and_beats.example: Halloran said, "Nobody is going to ask you about the March file."
tags_and_beats.effect: Useful when the speaker is new to the scene, or when the line would be misassigned without warning.
tags_and_beats.caution: It spends the line's surprise in advance; in a fast exchange it flattens every entry to the same shape.

tags_and_beats.name: medial tag
tags_and_beats.definition: Attribution inserted between two parts of one utterance, at the place where the speaker would draw breath.
tags_and_beats.example: "I signed it," she said, "the way I signed everything that year."
tags_and_beats.effect: Attributes early enough to be useful and creates a pause the punctuation alone could not.
tags_and_beats.caution: Break at a clause boundary. A tag dropped mid-phrase reads as an interruption the speaker did not make.

tags_and_beats.name: late tag
tags_and_beats.definition: Attribution arriving after a long line whose speaker the reader has already assigned, so the tag either confirms what was obvious or forces a re-read.
tags_and_beats.example: Weak: "Nobody in this building has read that file since the spring, and I include the people who signed it, and I include myself," said Halloran. Fixed: front the tag, or beat the line's opening.
tags_and_beats.effect: At best redundant; at worst it corrects the reader's assumption three clauses too late.
tags_and_beats.caution: Deliberate late attribution is a real device when the speaker's identity is the reveal — but then it is a reveal, and needs a paragraph of its own.

tags_and_beats.name: re-anchoring tag
tags_and_beats.definition: A single tag dropped back into a long untagged run to reset the reader's count of who is speaking.
tags_and_beats.example:
"You could have called."
"At two in the morning."
"At any hour you liked."
"And said what?" she said. "That I had read it?"
tags_and_beats.effect: Buys another eight lines of tagless speed for the price of two words.
tags_and_beats.caution: Anchor on the line that would be ambiguous, not the line that happens to be fourth; count the alternation yourself before deciding the reader can.

tags_and_beats.name: untagged volley
tags_and_beats.definition: A run of lines between two established speakers carried by strict alternation alone, with no tags and no beats.
tags_and_beats.example:
"You signed it."
"I signed a lot of things."
"You signed this one twice."
tags_and_beats.effect: Strips an exchange to pure speed; the reader hears the scene instead of watching it.
tags_and_beats.caution: Two speakers, short lines, no interruptions to the alternation — and re-anchor before the reader can lose the count.

tags_and_beats.name: name in the line
tags_and_beats.definition: Using a vocative inside the spoken line to identify who is being addressed, and by implication who is speaking.
tags_and_beats.example: "Marie, look at the date on it."
tags_and_beats.effect: Attributes and orients a three-way scene without a tag, and marks the moment one character singles another out.
tags_and_beats.caution: People use names far less than dialogue does — mostly to summon, warn, or wound. Reserve it for those.

tags_and_beats.name: vocative overuse
tags_and_beats.definition: Salting names through an exchange so the reader can keep track, until characters address each other more often than people do.
tags_and_beats.example: Weak: "I don't know, Marie." "You do know, Frank." "Marie." "Frank." Fixed: keep the first, cut the rest, add one beat.
tags_and_beats.effect: Reads as radio drama or as a hostage video; it also drains the vocative of the force it should have when it matters.
tags_and_beats.caution: Count the vocatives in any exchange over ten lines; more than two is almost always the tracking problem in disguise.

tags_and_beats.name: ambiguous attribution
tags_and_beats.definition: A line whose speaker cannot be determined from the paragraph it sits in — usually a beat by one character in the same paragraph as another character's speech.
tags_and_beats.example: Broken: "You should tell them." Halloran looked at the door. (Whose line?) Fixed: split the paragraph, or give the line the tag.
tags_and_beats.effect: Stops the reader mid-scene to audit the last six lines; nothing else in dialogue costs more attention.
tags_and_beats.caution: Most common after an interruption breaks the alternation, and in three-handers where the reader is tracking two possible answerers.

tags_and_beats.name: stage-direction pileup
tags_and_beats.definition: Stacking blocking, gesture, and facial description around every line until the choreography outweighs the talk.
tags_and_beats.example: Weak: She stood, crossed to the window, folded her arms, and turned back before she said, "No." Fixed: She went to the window. "No."
tags_and_beats.effect: Turns a scene into a rehearsal script; the reader loses the thread of the argument between the movements.
tags_and_beats.caution: Readers infer position from very little. Give one physical fact per exchange and let the rest stay unspecified.

typography_of_speech.name: cut-off dash
typography_of_speech.definition: An em dash at the end of a quotation marking speech severed by an interruption, an event, or the speaker's own stop.
typography_of_speech.example:
"If you had told me before the board met—"
"I tried to tell you in March."
typography_of_speech.effect: The line stops rather than fades; the reader hears the collision.
typography_of_speech.caution: The dash goes inside the closing quotation mark, with no comma. A tag after it starts a new sentence.

typography_of_speech.name: trailing ellipsis
typography_of_speech.definition: An ellipsis closing a quotation to mark speech that fades, wanders, or is abandoned by the speaker rather than cut off by another.
typography_of_speech.example: "I suppose if the dates were wrong then the whole schedule would…" She stopped and started again.
typography_of_speech.effect: Renders a speaker losing the thread, softening, or declining to finish; the drift is the characterization.
typography_of_speech.caution: Three or four on a page makes every character sound tentative; it is the single most overused mark in draft dialogue.

typography_of_speech.name: cut-versus-fade convention
typography_of_speech.definition: The house rule distinguishing the two marks: a dash for speech stopped from outside, an ellipsis for speech that runs down from inside.
typography_of_speech.example: Cut: "But the ledger says—" "The ledger is wrong." Fade: "But the ledger says…" Nobody finished it for her.
typography_of_speech.effect: Once applied consistently, the punctuation alone tells the reader whether the speaker was overruled or gave up.
typography_of_speech.caution: Mixing the two within a book teaches the reader nothing; pick the convention early and note it in the style sheet.

typography_of_speech.name: resumed line after interruption
typography_of_speech.definition: Rendering a speaker who is cut off and then picks the sentence back up, dash closing the first fragment and opening the resumption.
typography_of_speech.example:
"What I am telling you is that the file—"
"Nobody cares about the file."
"—the file was signed out to you."
typography_of_speech.effect: Shows a speaker refusing to be derailed; the syntax of the resumed clause proves the sentence was held in mind through the interruption.
typography_of_speech.caution: Only works if the resumed fragment is grammatically continuous with the first; readers check.

typography_of_speech.name: dash-initial dialogue
typography_of_speech.definition: A quotation convention using an opening dash for each speech and no quotation marks, common in French, Spanish, and Irish practice.
typography_of_speech.example:
— You signed for it, he said.
— I signed for a box. I did not open the box.
typography_of_speech.effect: Puts speech and narration on the same typographic plane; the page reads as one continuous voice.
typography_of_speech.caution: Nested quotation and mid-line narration become genuinely hard; commit to it for the whole book or not at all.

typography_of_speech.name: unquoted dialogue
typography_of_speech.definition: Running speech with no quotation marks and no dashes at all, distinguished from narration by paragraphing and diction alone.
typography_of_speech.example:
He asked her when she had last seen the file.
In March, she said. Before any of this.
And you signed it.
I signed it.
typography_of_speech.effect: Dissolves the boundary between narration and speech; the effect is incantatory and slightly unmoored.
typography_of_speech.caution: Requires short scenes, few speakers, and no interior quotation; and it costs the reader real work, which the prose must repay.

typography_of_speech.name: quotation within quotation
typography_of_speech.definition: A speaker quoting another speaker, marked with the alternate quotation mark inside the outer pair.
typography_of_speech.example: "He looked at me and said, 'That is not the number I gave the auditors,' and then he left."
typography_of_speech.effect: Lets a character stage a scene inside their own line — the most compact form of reported speech available in dialogue.
typography_of_speech.caution: Two nestings deep is the practical limit in prose, and single-inside-double is the American convention; the British house reverses it.

typography_of_speech.name: new speaker, new paragraph
typography_of_speech.definition: The base convention of English dialogue typography: each change of speaker starts a new paragraph, along with that speaker's beats and interiority.
typography_of_speech.example:
"You could have said something." She did not turn around.
"I did say something." He waited. "You were in Brussels."
typography_of_speech.effect: Does most of the attribution work in any well-set exchange, which is why tagless dialogue is legible at all.
typography_of_speech.caution: Violating it is not a stylistic choice but an ambiguity; if two speakers must share a paragraph, both need tags.

typography_of_speech.name: continuing-quotation open quote
typography_of_speech.definition: When one speaker's turn runs to several paragraphs, each new paragraph opens with a quotation mark and only the final paragraph closes one.
typography_of_speech.example:
"It started with the March schedule.

"By June there were two of them, and by the time anyone asked, only one had a signature on it."
typography_of_speech.effect: Signals a long unbroken turn without letting the reader assume the speaker changed.
typography_of_speech.caution: A turn long enough to need this is long enough to need auditing — see whether it is a monologue disguised as dialogue.

typography_of_speech.name: italics for unspoken speech
typography_of_speech.definition: Setting remembered lines, imagined speech, telepathy, or speech in another language in italics rather than quotation marks.
typography_of_speech.example: She heard it again in her father's voice. Sign nothing you have not read.
typography_of_speech.effect: Marks the line as not present in the room while keeping its full grammatical force as speech.
typography_of_speech.caution: One italic job per book. If italics already carry direct thought, they cannot also carry memory, emphasis, and the foreign language without collapsing.

typography_of_speech.name: capitals for volume
typography_of_speech.definition: Full capitals or small capitals used to render shouting, amplified announcement, or non-human voice.
typography_of_speech.example: The tannoy came on. ALL PASSENGERS FOR THE 6:40 SERVICE.
typography_of_speech.effect: Renders loudness typographically when the prose cannot afford to say it.
typography_of_speech.caution: In character speech it almost always reads as comic; small caps for institutional or machine voice survive better than capitals for anger.

typography_of_speech.name: phonetic respelling
typography_of_speech.definition: Spelling a speaker's words as they sound — wuz, gonna, tuh, 'orrible — to mark accent or class.
typography_of_speech.example: Weak: "Ah don't rightly know wot 'e wuz doin' wiv it." Fixed: "I don't rightly know what he was doing with it." — the syntax and the 'rightly' carry the voice.
typography_of_speech.effect: Slows reading, and marks the respelled speaker as deviant from an unmarked standard the narrator quietly occupies.
typography_of_speech.caution: Carry dialect in word choice, idiom, and syntax instead; reserve spelling for the one or two words that cannot be got any other way.

typography_of_speech.name: question mark inside the quotation
typography_of_speech.definition: Terminal question and exclamation marks belong inside the closing quotation mark when they belong to the quoted utterance, and the tag that follows stays lowercase.
typography_of_speech.effect: Keeps the mark with the speech act it modifies.
typography_of_speech.caution: The tag is not capitalized after a question mark — it is still the same sentence. This is the most-missed rule in draft dialogue.

typography_of_speech.name: comma before the tag
typography_of_speech.definition: A declarative quotation takes a comma, not a period, before an attributive tag — and a period, not a comma, before an action beat.
typography_of_speech.example:
"The file was never logged," she said.
"The file was never logged." She stood up.
typography_of_speech.effect: The punctuation tells the reader whether what follows is speech machinery or scene.
typography_of_speech.caution: The comma splice with a beat — "The file was never logged," she stood up — is the commonest mechanical error in dialogue.

typography_of_speech.name: solo line paragraph
typography_of_speech.definition: A single unattributed line of speech given its own paragraph with no tag, beat, or narration around it.
typography_of_speech.example:
They went through the schedule twice more and found nothing.

"Somebody moved it."

Neither of them said anything for a while.
typography_of_speech.effect: The white space above and below makes the line land like a struck note; ideal for the line that changes the scene.
typography_of_speech.caution: Only when the speaker is unmistakable, and once per scene — the device is entirely made of its own rarity.

typography_of_speech.name: set-off speech block
typography_of_speech.definition: A long speech rendered as an indented block without quotation marks, the way documentary and oral-history prose sets testimony.
typography_of_speech.example:
She gave the account she had given the auditors, in the same order:

    I opened the box in March. There was one schedule in it. I signed the cover sheet and sent the box back the same afternoon.
typography_of_speech.effect: Marks a turn as testimony or document rather than conversation, and licenses a length no exchange would tolerate.
typography_of_speech.register: narrative nonfiction, oral history, documentary fiction
typography_of_speech.caution: In fiction it breaks the scene frame — the reader hears an archive, not a room.

typography_of_speech.name: message-thread formatting
typography_of_speech.definition: Rendering texts, chat, or email in a distinct typographic treatment — sans-serif block, timestamps, alternating indent — rather than as quoted speech.
typography_of_speech.example:
22:14  you up
    22:51  i saw the march file
    22:51  call me
typography_of_speech.effect: Reproduces the medium's own silences: the delay between messages is on the page, and unanswered lines stay visibly unanswered.
typography_of_speech.caution: Check what the treatment costs in EPUB and in print at trim size; elaborate chat styling is the most common reflow casualty.

exchange_shapes.name: stichomythia
exchange_shapes.definition: Alternating single lines of roughly equal length between two speakers, each line answering the shape of the one before it.
exchange_shapes.example:
"You knew in March."
"I knew in April."
"You signed in March."
"I signed what they sent."
exchange_shapes.effect: Formalizes an argument into something closer to duel than conversation; the symmetry itself reads as pressure.
exchange_shapes.caution: Borrowed from verse drama; more than eight lines and prose starts to sound like a chant.

exchange_shapes.name: ping-pong exchange
exchange_shapes.definition: A run of short paired lines — statement, riposte, statement, riposte — with tags stripped to the minimum and no beats.
exchange_shapes.example:
"Where is it?"
"Filed."
"Filed where?"
"Wherever you put it."
exchange_shapes.effect: The fastest gear dialogue has; length on the page collapses while scene time speeds up.
exchange_shapes.caution: It cannot carry information the reader has not already got. Use it for pressure, then break out to a beat before anything must be understood.

exchange_shapes.name: shortening-line escalation
exchange_shapes.definition: An exchange whose lines get measurably shorter as the conflict rises, until the speakers are trading single words.
exchange_shapes.example:
"I would have told you if there had been anything worth telling."
"You had six weeks."
"I had nothing."
"You had this."
"No."
exchange_shapes.effect: Puts the escalation in the typography; the reader feels the acceleration before registering the content.
exchange_shapes.caution: It has one direction. Plan where the floor is, because after the one-word lines the only move left is silence or an act.

exchange_shapes.name: elliptical exchange
exchange_shapes.definition: An exchange in which each turn omits what the previous turn established, so the lines are grammatical fragments that only cohere as a pair.
exchange_shapes.effect: Renders long-standing intimacy or long-standing habit — people who have stopped supplying each other with context.
exchange_shapes.caution: Only between characters with a shared history the reader has; between strangers it reads as an author saving keystrokes.

exchange_shapes.name: three-hander tagging
exchange_shapes.definition: The attribution discipline a three-way scene requires: alternation no longer identifies anyone, so every turn needs a tag, a beat, a vocative, or an unmistakable idiom.
exchange_shapes.example:
"Somebody signed it." Halloran did not look up from the folder.
"Not me," said Marie.
"Nobody said you, Marie."
"You looked at me when you said somebody."
exchange_shapes.effect: Keeps three voices separable at speed; the vocative and the idiom do the work the alternation did in a two-hander.
exchange_shapes.caution: Give the third party a stake and a syntax of their own, or the scene silently becomes a two-hander with a witness.

exchange_shapes.name: designated silent party
exchange_shapes.definition: A group scene in which one present character is given no lines, their silence tracked by beats until it becomes the scene's loudest element.
exchange_shapes.example: The three of them worked through the schedule for an hour. Marie, who had signed all of it, refilled the water twice and said nothing.
exchange_shapes.effect: Concentrates the reader's attention on the one person not talking; the eventual first line arrives with everything behind it.
exchange_shapes.caution: The silence must be visibly maintained — one beat every half page — or the reader simply forgets the character is in the room.

exchange_shapes.name: rendered overlap
exchange_shapes.definition: Two speakers talking at once, rendered by interleaved fragments, a bracketed simultaneity note, or a dash-and-resume pattern rather than by narration.
exchange_shapes.example:
"—and I have said twice now that the file—"
"—nobody is accusing you—"
"—that the file was not in the box."
exchange_shapes.effect: Puts the collision on the page; the reader's difficulty in parsing it is the point.
exchange_shapes.caution: Prose has no real simultaneity. Two or three lines is the ceiling before the reader stops and re-reads.

exchange_shapes.name: interrogation ladder
exchange_shapes.definition: A questioning exchange built as a rising series — each answer narrowing the ground for the next question — with the decisive question held for last.
exchange_shapes.example:
"You logged the box."
"Yes."
"You logged it on the twelfth."
"If that's what it says."
"The box was collected on the ninth."
exchange_shapes.effect: Gives a question scene a shape the reader can feel closing; each rung removes an answer that was available a moment ago.
exchange_shapes.caution: The interesting version is the one where the questioner is also learning; a ladder whose answers are all foreknown is a lecture in question form.

exchange_shapes.name: one-sided phone call
exchange_shapes.definition: A telephone exchange rendered from one end only, the other party's turns inferable from the pauses and from what the audible speaker answers.
exchange_shapes.example: "No. No, she left in March." A pause. "Because I signed the exit form myself." Longer. "Then somebody has two of them."
exchange_shapes.effect: Makes the reader do the reconstruction, which is more engaging than hearing both halves; it also withholds the other party's tone.
exchange_shapes.caution: The audible speaker must not repeat the question back for the reader's benefit — that is the tell that turns the device into exposition.

exchange_shapes.name: epistolary exchange
exchange_shapes.definition: A conversation conducted across documents — letters, memos, emails — where each turn is composed, dated, and aware of its own record.
exchange_shapes.example:
Re: March schedule (2 Apr): As discussed, please confirm the cover sheet was signed in your presence.
Re: Re: March schedule (2 Apr): I have no recollection of the conversation you are describing.
exchange_shapes.effect: Every turn is performed for a future reader, which lets subtext live in formality, in the timestamp, and in what is quoted back.
exchange_shapes.caution: The delay between turns is the medium's whole rhythm; collapse it and the exchange becomes ordinary dialogue in bad clothes.

exchange_shapes.name: text-message exchange
exchange_shapes.definition: A conversation in short asynchronous messages, where read receipts, delay, typing indicators, and deleted drafts are available as turns.
exchange_shapes.example:
did you send it
    yes
    to who
    [typing]
    to who
exchange_shapes.effect: Silence is timestamped and therefore unmistakable; a repeated unanswered line does work no spoken exchange can do.
exchange_shapes.caution: Register is the whole characterization here — punctuation, capitalization, and message length carry what voice carries elsewhere.

exchange_shapes.name: transcript rendering
exchange_shapes.definition: An exchange presented in the format of a record — speaker labels, line numbers, inaudible markers — rather than as narrated scene.
exchange_shapes.example:
Q. And you signed the cover sheet.
A. I signed something that afternoon.
Q. The cover sheet.
A. [inaudible]
exchange_shapes.effect: Strips every beat and tag away and forces the reader to hear only the words, which makes evasion far more visible.
exchange_shapes.caution: Its flatness is the effect; used twice in a book it becomes a formatting habit rather than an argument.

exchange_shapes.name: monologue interrupted
exchange_shapes.definition: A long turn deliberately broken once or twice by another speaker, so the length is dramatized as something the room is tolerating.
exchange_shapes.example:
"—and by the time anyone opened the second box—"
"There was a second box."
"There were always two boxes. As I have been saying."
exchange_shapes.effect: Converts a speech into a scene: the interruptions establish the audience and give the speaker something to push against.
exchange_shapes.caution: The interruption must cost the speaker something; a listener who only says 'go on' is a stenographer.

exchange_shapes.name: aborted exchange
exchange_shapes.definition: A conversation that never reaches its subject — opened, deflected once, and abandoned by mutual consent.
exchange_shapes.example:
"About March—"
"Do you want the good chair or that one?"
"That one's fine."
exchange_shapes.effect: Shows two people agreeing not to have the scene; the reader carries the unhad conversation forward as pressure.
exchange_shapes.caution: Needs the reader to know what was avoided; without that it reads as a scene the writer lost interest in.

exchange_shapes.name: choral reply
exchange_shapes.definition: A crowd answering as one voice, rendered as a single quoted line attributed to the group or reported as unison.
exchange_shapes.example:
"Who authorized it?" Halloran said, to the room.
Nobody said anything, and then four people said Marie.
exchange_shapes.effect: Turns a crowd into a character for one line; the unison is either comic or menacing and rarely anything in between.
exchange_shapes.caution: Once per scene, and never for information — a crowd cannot deliver an explanation without becoming absurd.

exchange_shapes.name: the relay
exchange_shapes.definition: A line passed along a chain of speakers — A tells B, B tells C — with the content changing slightly at each handoff.
exchange_shapes.example:
"He says the box was collected on the ninth."
"She says he says it was the ninth."
"So somebody is saying the ninth."
exchange_shapes.effect: Dramatizes distortion and distance in a single exchange, and lets the reader watch a fact become a rumor.

exchange_shapes.name: nested exchange
exchange_shapes.definition: A conversation reported inside a conversation, one speaker performing both halves of an earlier scene for a present listener.
exchange_shapes.example: "So I said, 'It was in the box,' and he said, 'Which box,' and I said, 'You know which box.'"
exchange_shapes.effect: Compresses a whole prior scene into one turn while characterizing the reporter through what they choose to reproduce.
exchange_shapes.caution: The reporter is an unreliable narrator by construction; if you do not want that, summarize instead.

exchange_shapes.name: the earned long turn
exchange_shapes.definition: A single extended speech placed after a scene of short exchange, its length licensed by everything that has been refused up to that point.
exchange_shapes.example: They had gone eight lines at four words each. Then Marie put both hands flat on the table and talked for a page and a half without being interrupted once.
exchange_shapes.effect: The shift in turn length is itself the event; the reader registers that something has broken open.
exchange_shapes.caution: Earned once per book, maybe twice. Placed early it is just a monologue.

subtext_techniques.name: answering the wrong question
subtext_techniques.definition: A speaker responds to a question adjacent to the one asked, and the gap between the two is where the meaning sits.
subtext_techniques.example:
"Did you read it before you signed it?"
"It was the last week of the quarter."
subtext_techniques.effect: The evasion is legible without being announced; the reader convicts the speaker without the narrator saying anything.
subtext_techniques.caution: The wrong answer must be a plausible answer to something, or it reads as a non sequitur rather than a dodge.

subtext_techniques.name: deflection by counter-question
subtext_techniques.definition: Returning a question instead of answering it, so the burden of the exchange moves back across the table.
subtext_techniques.example:
"Where did the second copy go?"
"Why are you asking me and not Halloran?"
subtext_techniques.effect: Buys the speaker a turn and tells the reader the answer exists and is being kept.
subtext_techniques.caution: Two in a row and the exchange stalls; the second question has to concede something or the scene stops moving.

subtext_techniques.name: refused beat
subtext_techniques.definition: A speaker declines the response their partner's turn requires — no answer to the greeting, no thanks for the offer, no laugh at the joke.
subtext_techniques.example:
"Good to see you again."
"You have the schedule?"
subtext_techniques.effect: Withholding the expected second half of a pair is the cheapest hostility in dialogue and needs no adverb at all.
subtext_techniques.caution: Readers notice the refusal only if the ritual was clearly invoked; establish the expected reply before you deny it.

subtext_techniques.name: displacement object
subtext_techniques.definition: Running an unspeakable subject through a mundane one, so the argument about the marriage is conducted entirely about the dishes.
subtext_techniques.example:
"You always leave the pan."
"I leave one pan."
"Every night, one pan, for someone else to find in the morning."
subtext_techniques.effect: Lets characters say the true thing with full heat while retaining deniability; the reader hears both conversations at once.
subtext_techniques.caution: The reader must already know the real subject. Establish it, then never name it inside the exchange.

subtext_techniques.name: the unspoken referent
subtext_techniques.definition: An exchange conducted entirely in pronouns and deictics — it, that, the whole thing — because naming the subject is what neither speaker will do.
subtext_techniques.example:
"Have you told him?"
"There's nothing to tell yet."
"There will be."
subtext_techniques.effect: The refusal to name is the characterization; the reader supplies the noun and is thereby implicated.
subtext_techniques.caution: The reader needs an antecedent from somewhere. Two floating referents in one scene and the scene is merely vague.

subtext_techniques.name: agreement that undercuts
subtext_techniques.definition: A speaker concedes in words while the terms of the concession withdraw everything it appeared to give.
subtext_techniques.example: "You're right. You've always been better with the paperwork than I am. That's why they gave it to you."
subtext_techniques.effect: Hostility rendered as compliance; there is nothing in the line to object to, which is the trap.
subtext_techniques.caution: Keep the sting in the specifics, not in the tone; a sarcastic delivery converts it into ordinary aggression.

subtext_techniques.name: over-politeness as hostility
subtext_techniques.definition: Escalating formality — full names, please and thank you, complete sentences — where the relationship licenses none.
subtext_techniques.example: "Thank you for the clarification, Mr. Halloran. I'll be sure to put it in writing."
subtext_techniques.effect: Signals that the relationship has been withdrawn; the courtesy is the announcement of it.
subtext_techniques.caution: Depends on an established informal baseline — the reader must have heard these two speak casually first.

subtext_techniques.name: the shared reference
subtext_techniques.definition: An allusion, nickname, or shorthand that both speakers understand fully and the reader decodes at partial strength.
subtext_techniques.example:
"It's Brussels again."
"It is not Brussels again."
"It is exactly Brussels again."
subtext_techniques.effect: Creates the intimacy of overheard talk; the reader's partial exclusion is the evidence that these two have a history.
subtext_techniques.caution: Decodable within a page or two. A reference the reader never gets is not intimacy, it is withheld information.

subtext_techniques.name: the true thing said as a joke
subtext_techniques.definition: A speaker delivers the thing they actually mean in a register that makes it retractable.
subtext_techniques.example: "You'd sign anything, wouldn't you." He laughed at the end of it, a half-beat late.
subtext_techniques.effect: Lets a confession or an accusation reach the room while both parties keep the option of not having heard it.
subtext_techniques.caution: The retraction option has to be visible — a laugh, a shrug, an immediate change of subject — or it is just an accusation.

subtext_techniques.name: the repeated word that shifts
subtext_techniques.definition: A single word passed back and forth across an exchange, arriving each time with a different weight.
subtext_techniques.example:
"It was routine."
"Routine."
"Routine. That's the word they used."
"That's the word you used."
subtext_techniques.effect: Makes the scene's argument audible as a contest over one term, with no narration required.
subtext_techniques.caution: Three appearances is the working maximum; the fourth turns the device into a chant.

subtext_techniques.name: the delayed answer
subtext_techniques.definition: A line that answers something said much earlier — pages or chapters back — without marking the connection.
subtext_techniques.example: "I read it," she said, apropos of nothing anyone in the room had raised. He knew exactly which sentence she meant.
subtext_techniques.effect: Proves that a character has been holding a scene in mind, and rewards the reader who has too.
subtext_techniques.caution: The original line must have been distinctive enough to be recalled; give it its own paragraph the first time.

subtext_techniques.name: the negation that confirms
subtext_techniques.definition: A denial that introduces the very thing nobody had raised, so the disclaimer becomes the disclosure.
subtext_techniques.example:
"This isn't about the money."
"Nobody mentioned money."
subtext_techniques.effect: Lets the reader catch what a character has just given away, one beat before the character does.
subtext_techniques.caution: Only lands if the other speaker declines to be polite about it — or pointedly says nothing at all.

subtext_techniques.name: the topic that will not stay changed
subtext_techniques.definition: One speaker steers away three times and the other steers back, until the returning itself is the scene's content.
subtext_techniques.example:
"How's the flat?"
"Fine. About March—"
"Did you get the boiler done?"
"About March."
subtext_techniques.effect: Dramatizes will without any narration of it; the reader counts the returns and knows who is going to win.
subtext_techniques.caution: Three returns is the shape. Two is a hiccup, five is a comedy sketch.

subtext_techniques.name: the answer aimed past the asker
subtext_techniques.definition: In a scene with three or more present, a character answers one person's question while directing the answer at another.
subtext_techniques.example:
"Was the box sealed when it came back?" Marie asked.
"It was sealed," Halloran said, looking at the auditor. "It was sealed when it left, too."
subtext_techniques.effect: Turns a two-person exchange into a three-person power scene without a line of explanation.
subtext_techniques.caution: Needs one beat of blocking — where the eyes go — and no more; the moment it is explained it stops working.

silence_and_pause.name: silence in the answer slot
silence_and_pause.definition: Leaving the responding turn structurally empty — a beat, a paragraph break, or a line of narration where the reply belonged.
silence_and_pause.example:
"Did you know before the board met?"
Outside, someone was locking up the bicycles.
"I'm going to take that as a yes."
silence_and_pause.effect: An unfilled reply slot is read as an answer, and usually as the worst available one.
silence_and_pause.caution: Only works where a reply was clearly owed; in a loose conversation a silence is just a gap.

silence_and_pause.name: the pause before capitulation
silence_and_pause.definition: A measured beat placed between the demand and the surrender, so the giving-in is visibly a decision.
silence_and_pause.example:
"Sign it."
She looked at the page for long enough that he started to speak again, and then she signed it.
silence_and_pause.effect: Buys the concession its cost; without the pause the character reads as having never held the position.
silence_and_pause.caution: Give the pause a physical duration the reader can measure — an action, a sound, a count — not the word 'finally'.

silence_and_pause.name: white space as pause
silence_and_pause.definition: Using paragraph break, extra leading, or a section break to time a silence typographically rather than describing it.
silence_and_pause.example:
"You could still withdraw it."


"No," he said. "I couldn't."
silence_and_pause.effect: The reader's eye travel becomes the pause; the effect is felt rather than reported.
silence_and_pause.caution: Vertical space is fragile in EPUB and reflowable formats; verify it survives the build before relying on it.

silence_and_pause.name: sustained refusal to speak
silence_and_pause.definition: A character present through a whole exchange who will not talk, their refusal maintained by beats and by other characters' reactions to it.
silence_and_pause.example: They asked her four times, in four different ways. She answered the first one with a shake of the head and the other three with nothing at all.
silence_and_pause.effect: Converts silence from absence into action; the refusing character is doing the most in the scene.
silence_and_pause.caution: Give the refusal a cost that mounts, or the scene stalls; someone must be losing something for every question that goes unanswered.

silence_and_pause.name: the broken silence
silence_and_pause.definition: The mechanics of who speaks first after a pause, and what that costs them.
silence_and_pause.example:
Neither of them said anything for the length of the platform announcement.
"All right," Halloran said, and by saying it first he had conceded the argument.
silence_and_pause.effect: Makes a pause into a contest with a winner; the reader learns the balance of the room from one line.
silence_and_pause.caution: State the cost once, then trust it. The device dies the moment the narration explains it a second time.

silence_and_pause.name: pause rendered as an action beat
silence_and_pause.definition: Timing a silence with a physical event of measurable duration instead of naming it as a pause.
silence_and_pause.example: Weak: There was a long pause. Fixed: She poured the rest of the water into the glass, and then into the other glass, and set the jug down.
silence_and_pause.effect: Gives the reader an actual duration rather than an assertion of one, and characterizes the waiting.
silence_and_pause.caution: The action must be idle; a beat that advances the plot fills the silence instead of measuring it.

silence_and_pause.name: the delayed reply
silence_and_pause.definition: An answer that arrives a full beat late, the lateness marked so the reader registers the interval as content.
silence_and_pause.example:
"You'd tell me if it was serious."
He finished the sentence he was writing.
"I'd tell you."
silence_and_pause.effect: The interval reads as calculation, reluctance, or the assembling of a lie — and the words alone would show none of it.
silence_and_pause.caution: Reserve it for lines whose content is otherwise unremarkable; on a dramatic line the delay is redundant.

silence_and_pause.name: the question left unanswered
silence_and_pause.definition: A question that the scene moves past without any reply at all, the narration declining to note the omission.
silence_and_pause.example:
"Whose initials are those?"
They worked through the rest of the box before the light went, and then they went home.
silence_and_pause.effect: Leaves the question live in the reader's hands rather than the characters'; it is still open pages later.
silence_and_pause.caution: Pay it off somewhere, or the reader files it as an authorial oversight rather than a character's evasion.

silence_and_pause.name: group silence around an exchange
silence_and_pause.definition: A two-person exchange conducted in front of witnesses whose collective silence is tracked as a presence.
silence_and_pause.example:
"Say it again," Marie said, "with everyone here."
Nobody at the table moved. Somebody's phone buzzed twice and was not picked up.
silence_and_pause.effect: Raises the stakes of every line by giving it an audience that will not intervene.
silence_and_pause.caution: Note the room twice at most; a witness beat after every line turns the crowd into a laugh track.

silence_and_pause.name: silence in an argumentative exchange
silence_and_pause.definition: In argument or nonfiction dialogue, the unanswered objection — the point conceded by no response rather than by agreement.
silence_and_pause.example:
"You have not addressed the third schedule."
"We should take the others in order."
silence_and_pause.effect: The gap is the argument's real result; readers of argument track unanswered points more reliably than answered ones.
silence_and_pause.caution: If the writer wants the silence read as a concession, some later line must treat it as one.

dialogue_faults.name: as-you-know-bob
dialogue_faults.definition: Characters tell each other things both already know, so the reader can overhear the exposition.
dialogue_faults.example: Broken: "As you know, Marie, the March schedule has to be countersigned by two directors." Fixed: give the information to someone who does not have it, or put it in narration.
dialogue_faults.effect: Breaks the reality of the scene at exactly the moment the writer needed the reader to believe it.
dialogue_faults.caution: The 'as you know' is only the visible marker; the fault survives every attempt to disguise it with a question mark.

dialogue_faults.name: on-the-nose dialogue
dialogue_faults.definition: Characters say exactly and only what they mean, with no gap between intention and utterance.
dialogue_faults.example: Broken: "I'm angry at you because you didn't defend me at the board meeting." Fixed: "How was the meeting?" "You'd know."
dialogue_faults.effect: Removes the reader's work and therefore the reader's engagement; every line is fully spent on arrival.
dialogue_faults.caution: Some characters and some genres are legitimately direct; the fault is when nobody in the book has an inside.

dialogue_faults.name: undifferentiated voices
dialogue_faults.definition: Every character speaks in the same syntax, vocabulary, and rhythm, so tags become the only means of telling them apart.
dialogue_faults.example: Test: strip every tag from a page of dialogue and hand it to a reader. If they cannot assign the lines, the voices are one voice.
dialogue_faults.effect: Forces heavy tagging, kills tagless exchange, and makes the cast feel like one author talking to himself.
dialogue_faults.caution: Differentiate by sentence length, register, and what each character will not say — not by tics and catchphrases.

dialogue_faults.name: dialogue as infodump
dialogue_faults.definition: A character delivers a paragraph of background, procedure, or history that the scene has no dramatic reason to contain.
dialogue_faults.example: Broken: three hundred words on how the countersignature process works, spoken by the one person with no reason to explain it. Fixed: cut to the two lines that matter to the listener.
dialogue_faults.effect: The scene stops; the reader can feel the author's hand on the character's mouth.
dialogue_faults.caution: If the information is genuinely needed, narration can deliver it in a third of the space and without the pretense.

dialogue_faults.name: over-tagged exchange
dialogue_faults.definition: Every line attributed, often with a beat as well, in a two-hander where alternation would have carried it.
dialogue_faults.example: Broken: "No," she said. "Why not?" he asked. "Because," she answered. Fixed: "No." "Why not?" "Because."
dialogue_faults.effect: Halves the pace of an exchange that was written to be fast.
dialogue_faults.caution: Usually a symptom of undifferentiated voices — the writer can feel that the lines are not self-identifying.

dialogue_faults.name: greeting preamble
dialogue_faults.definition: Starting a dialogue scene at the hellos, so the reader sits through arrival, coats, and weather before the scene begins.
dialogue_faults.example: Broken: "Hi." "Hi. Come in." "Thanks. Filthy out there." "Coffee?" Fixed: open on "You should have called me first."
dialogue_faults.effect: Spends the reader's attention on the least loaded lines in the scene.
dialogue_faults.caution: Ritual openings earn their place only when the ritual is being violated or refused.

dialogue_faults.name: unmotivated topic switch
dialogue_faults.definition: A speaker changes subject with no pressure, deflection, or interruption to license it, because the writer needed the next topic.
dialogue_faults.example: Broken: "I signed it in March." "Do you still see your brother?" Fixed: give the switch a motive, and let the other speaker notice it.
dialogue_faults.effect: Readers track conversational coherence closely; an unmotivated jump registers as a manuscript seam.
dialogue_faults.caution: Motivated switches are a fine device — deflection, exhaustion, cruelty — but the other character has to react to them.

dialogue_faults.name: monologue disguised as dialogue
dialogue_faults.definition: One character talks for pages while another supplies 'go on', 'I see', and 'what happened then'.
dialogue_faults.example: Broken: "And then?" "Then the second box arrived." "Go on." Fixed: cut the prompter, set it as a block, or give the listener a stake.
dialogue_faults.effect: The quotation marks are doing nothing but disguising narration as scene.
dialogue_faults.caution: Either make the listener a participant with something to lose, or stop pretending and use narration.

dialogue_faults.name: dialect overload
dialogue_faults.definition: Rendering a speaker's variety so thoroughly — respellings, apostrophes, glossed idiom — that reading becomes decoding.
dialogue_faults.example: Broken: a page of apostrophes and dropped consonants. Fixed: two markers of syntax and one of idiom, then let the reader hold the voice.
dialogue_faults.effect: Exhausts the reader and, applied to only some characters, quietly marks those characters as other.
dialogue_faults.caution: The modern practice is light and syntactic; if you must be heavy, be heavy for everyone including the narrator.

dialogue_faults.name: quip that stops the scene
dialogue_faults.definition: A joke placed where the scene's pressure was building, releasing it and leaving the exchange with nowhere to go.
dialogue_faults.example: Broken: "You knew and you said nothing." "I say nothing beautifully. It's my one skill." Fixed: hold the quip until the pressure has paid out.
dialogue_faults.effect: Trades a scene's accumulated tension for one line's return, usually a bad exchange rate.
dialogue_faults.caution: The same joke three lines later, after the confrontation lands, often works — it is placement, not the joke.

dialogue_faults.name: dialogue summarizing an off-page scene
dialogue_faults.definition: Characters recount to each other an event the reader did not witness, in the level of detail only a narrator would supply.
dialogue_faults.example: Broken: "So I went in, and he was at the desk, and he said the box had been logged twice…" Fixed: dramatize the scene, or report it in narration in two sentences.
dialogue_faults.effect: Asks the reader to sit through a scene at second hand, with the tension already resolved.
dialogue_faults.caution: Legitimate when the telling is itself the event — a lie, a confession, a version being constructed for a listener.

dialogue_faults.name: floating heads
dialogue_faults.definition: A long exchange with no beats, no setting, and no bodies, so the voices talk in an unplaceable void.
dialogue_faults.example: Broken: forty lines of tagless dialogue with no indication of where anyone is. Fixed: one physical anchor every eight to ten lines.
dialogue_faults.effect: The reader loses the room, then the blocking, then the count of who is speaking.
dialogue_faults.caution: The fix is one physical fact, not a paragraph of description; the fault is absence, and its opposite is stage-direction pileup.

dialogue_faults.name: too-cooperative dialogue
dialogue_faults.definition: Every question gets its answer, every request is granted, and no one misunderstands anything.
dialogue_faults.example: Broken: "Where's the file?" "In the second box." "Can I see it?" "Of course." Fixed: make one of those refusals, and one a misunderstanding.
dialogue_faults.effect: Removes friction from the only part of the book made of friction; the exchange becomes an information transfer.
dialogue_faults.caution: Real conversation is full of partial answers, mishearings, and questions nobody bothers to answer.

dialogue_faults.name: unearned eloquence
dialogue_faults.definition: Every character speaks in balanced, fully formed periods regardless of pressure, education, or how fast the scene is moving.
dialogue_faults.example: Broken: a panicked witness producing three subordinate clauses in sequence. Fixed: fragments, repetition, and one sentence that never gets finished.
dialogue_faults.effect: Flattens the cast toward the author's own written register and drains urgency out of every high-pressure scene.
dialogue_faults.caution: Some characters are genuinely eloquent; the test is whether pressure changes anyone's syntax.

dialogue_faults.name: uncontracted speech
dialogue_faults.definition: Dialogue written without contractions or fragments, so characters speak the way documents are written.
dialogue_faults.example: Broken: "I do not know what you are referring to and I would not have signed it." Fixed: "I don't know what you mean. And I wouldn't have signed it."
dialogue_faults.effect: Makes every speaker sound either foreign, robotic, or under oath, and does so without meaning to.
dialogue_faults.caution: Full forms are a real device for emphasis, formality, and denial — 'I did not sign it' — which only works if the baseline is contracted.
